Every town has one door that no one notices until they need it. In my town, it stood between the bakery and the closed cinema, painted the green of old bottles. Above it, a brass sign read: REPAIRS.

I went there carrying my grandfather’s watch, which had stopped during a thunderstorm. Inside, an old woman sat beneath hundreds of ticking clocks, though none showed the same hour.

“Time is rarely broken,” she said. “Usually, it is only waiting.”

She opened the watch and removed a speck of blue light. The room darkened. Somewhere outside, rain began falling upward.

While she worked, I wandered between shelves crowded with unlikely objects: a jar labeled almost, a suitcase full of warm wind, three apologies folded into paper boats. Each seemed familiar, as if I had lost it years ago without noticing.

When the watch started again, its ticking sounded different. Not faster or slower, but kinder.

The woman refused payment. Instead, she asked me to leave something on a shelf by the door. I searched my pockets and found only a bus ticket, a button, and the memory of being seven, hiding beneath the kitchen table while my grandfather pretended not to see me.

I left the memory.

Outside, the cinema lights were burning. People hurried past, dry beneath clear skies. I never found the green door again, but sometimes, when the watch ticks, I hear distant laughter, and a small hand gently knocking beneath a table, waiting patiently to be found again.
